C005.subject: household electricity consumption per capita
C005.predicate: is a more accurate proxy for
C005.object: average material consumption in developed economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: household electricity consumption per capita average material consumption in developed economies]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Material Resources Productivity and Household Electricity Consumption Panel Data Analysis (2000-2023) — Panel regression comparing per capita household electricity consumption with direct material consumption (DMC) across OECD countries can test correlation strength and proxy validity, controlling for income, climate, and energy mix.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on energy-material decoupling in developed economies — Reviewing studies on the relationship between electricity use and material footprint, especially those addressing the rebound effect and service economy shifts, can assess whether electricity remains a reliable proxy amid structural changes.

[PATH:theoretical] Input-Output Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) linking household electricity use to embodied material flows — Constructing a theoretical model that maps electricity consumption to material supply chains (e.g., through input-output tables) can formally evaluate the mechanistic plausibility of the proxy, accounting for indirect material use in electronics and appliances.

C006.subject: GDP per capita
C006.object: average material consumption in developed economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita average material consumption in developed economies]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index microdata on material consumption per capita vs. GDP per capita for OECD countries (2020-2023) — Directly compares actual household material consumption (e.g., food, housing, durables) with GDP per capita across the domain, enabling quantitative correlation tests to confirm or refute the measure's reliability.

[PATH:literature] Review of literature on the 'Beyond GDP' agenda, e.g., Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission reports (2009) and follow-ups (2020 onwards) — Provides established theoretical and empirical critiques of GDP per capita as a welfare/consumption proxy, evaluating its validity in developed economies with non-market services, inequality adjustments, and public goods.

[PATH:empirical] Cross-national panel regression of household final consumption expenditure (HFCE) vs. GDP per capita in OECD nations, controlling for income distribution and non-market production — Tests whether GDP per capita systematically over- or underestimates average material consumption when accounting for savings, public services, and home production, using World Bank/UN data from 2020 onward.

C007.subject: Comprehensive wealth indicators (e.g., inclusive wealth)
C007.object: long-term consumption sustainability better than GDP in nations with high natural capital depletion
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Comprehensive wealth indicators (e.g., inclusive wealth) long-term consumption sustainability better than GDP in nations with high natural capital depletion]

[PATH:empirical] World Bank's Changing Wealth of Nations dataset (2005-2020) – longitudinal inclusive wealth accounts including natural capital, produced capital, and human capital — Directly tests whether comprehensive wealth changes correlate with future consumption sustainability (e.g., genuine savings or adjusted net savings) in resource-dependent economies, compared to GDP growth trajectories.

[PATH:theoretical] Arrow et al. (2012) 'Sustainability and the Measurement of Wealth' (Environment and Development Economics) – theoretical framework linking comprehensive wealth to intergenerational consumption possibility frontier — Provides the foundational theory that inclusive wealth should predict sustainable consumption when natural capital is depleted, enabling derivation of testable hypotheses against GDP-based measures.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of resource-dependent nations (e.g., Botswana vs. Nigeria, 2005-2020) using inclusive wealth and consumption data from UNEP's Inclusive Wealth Report — Empirical contrast of high natural capital depletion countries with divergent consumption trends; isolates whether wealth metrics outperform GDP in signalling future consumption declines.

qualifier.geographic: nations with high natural capital depletion (e.g., resource-dependent economies)

C008.subject: Comprehensive wealth indicators (e.g., inclusive wealth)
C008.object: true economic wellbeing because their valuation of natural and human capital is inherently subjective and politically manipulable
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Comprehensive wealth indicators (e.g., inclusive wealth) true economic wellbeing because their valuation of natural and human capital is inherently subjective and politically manipulable]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative analysis of Inclusive Wealth Index (IWI) and genuine savings (GS) vs. subjective well-being surveys (e.g., Gallup, World Happiness Report) across OECD and emerging economies (2000-2020) — This would empirically test whether comprehensive wealth indicators correlate with direct measures of perceived wellbeing; weak or inconsistent correlations would support the hypothesis that subjective valuation and political manipulation distort the indicator.

[PATH:empirical] Political economy case studies of contested natural capital valuation in national wealth accounts (e.g., Norway's oil fund vs. Brazil's rainforest valuation) showing manipulation or revision of shadow prices over time — These cases can reveal the extent to which the valuation of natural and human capital is politically manipulable, thereby confirming the hypothesis's key claim about inherent subjectivity and political influence.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical literature on commensurability and multidimensional welfare measurement (e.g., Dasgupta, 2009; Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi, 2009) critiquing the normative assumptions behind shadow pricing of environmental and human capital — A review of this literature will clarify whether the subjectivity and manipulability are inherent to the methodology or can be mitigated, thus refuting or supporting the hypothesis on conceptual grounds.

qualifier.geographic: global, with particular relevance to OECD countries and emerging economies
